speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the bill?
On division.
Can the minister give us any information on the present state of the United States loan to Britain? Has he any information beyond what has appeared in the press?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not know how it is getting along or what the prospects are, but I am hopeful.

The opinion seems to be that the legislation will pass congress and the loan be made. But in the event that it should not pass and the loan not be made, can the minister tell us briefly what the effect would be with respect to our loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By section 8 our act will not come into force until there is a proclamation, and that may apply to any portion of the act. The result of the defeat of the loan in the United States would in all probability be that we would not proclaim certain sections of this act. Probably it would be well for me to read again the letter that I wrote to the chancellor of the exchequer covering the situation that might arise. It is as follows:
Ottawa, 6th March, 1916. Dear Chancellor of the Exchequer,
On the occasion of the signature of the financial agreement between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada, I should like to place on record our understanding regarding the entry into force and implementation of this agreement in relation to the action by the United States congress on the financial agreement between the government of the United Kingdom and the government of the United States, signed at Washington on December, 1915.
The agreement between the United Kingdom and Canada has been drawn up in the expectation that the Anglo-American agreement will be approved by congress and will enter into force some time during the current year. If, however, congress does not approve the Anglo-American agreement, our understanding is that, in the terms of article 8 of our agreement, a major change would1 have occurred it the international financial situation, which would materially alter prospective benefits and obligations flowing from our agreement, and that consequently it would be necessary forthwith to consider what changes in the provisions of our agreement the two governments should agree to make, subject to such legislative approval as may be necessary. In these circumstances, it is also our understanding that articles 5, 6 and 7 of our agreement will not be implemented until it is known whether the United States congress has approved the Anglo-American agreement. I agree, however, that these articles are to be implemented immediately congress approves that agreement.
I should appreciate it if you would confirm that the above understanding is in accordance with that of your government.
Yours very truly,
J. L. Ilsley.
Article 5 is the article relating to exchange and import arrangements; article 6 is our agreement to extend the 1942 loan for another five years interest-free; and article 7 is our cancellation of the commonwealth air training plan. These are not going to be brought into force until we know what happens to the loan in the United States.
Will this Canadian loan be made regardless of whether or not the United States loan is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not certain. It is open to us to draw back on that under article 8. Naturally, purchases are being financed at the present time and some money will be advanced .after this legislation goes through, even before we know whether the United States loan will go through or not. But it would be open to us to draw back if the loan in the United States did not go through because the defeat of the loan in the United States would be a major change in the international financial situation which would materially alter prospective benefits and obligations flowing from our agreement. Consequently it would be necessary to consider forthwith what changes in the provisions of our agreement the two governments should agree to make subject to such legislative approval as may be necessary. Legally I do not know just what the position would be should the United Kingdom not agree to make these changes, but I know that the relations between the two governments are such that the legal feature would be immaterial. The United Kingdom government understand, and so state in their confirmation of our understanding in this letter, that we have done all this on the expectation that the loan would go through in the United States. If it does not, there is a major change. The main benefits we can expect to get from this loan are dependent upon the loan going through in the United States, thus putting the United Kingdom in a position to be an expanding and reliable market, something that is of great advantage to the United States as it is to us.

The minister has explained what the law permits the government to do in the event that the United States loan is not made. My question was simply this, and I do not think the minister is trying to evade it: If the United States loan to Britain rs not made, will our loan still be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We would immediately have to get in touch with the United Kingdom and consider the situation. I cannot say whether the full amount of the loan in that event would be made or not. Quite a lot of money would already have been advanced

Loan to United Kingdom
by that time anyway, and whether we would saw it off then or go the full way is something that would have to be taken up at that time. I cannot commit the government on that.
The position, then, is this. Once this measure passes these two houses, the government will be enabled to make a loan of 11,250,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And will be bound to make it if the United States loan goes through.

In the event of the failure of the other loan, you will not be bound to make any part of our loan save what has
been already advanced.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know exactly what the legal position is as between us and the United Kingdom because the undertaking is one that must be carefully considered when the situation arises. But, whatever the legal position is, I would say that is substantially the situation, that we would then be free- perhaps not legally as between ourselves and the United Kingdom but we would be free within the spirit of the understanding-to say, , "No; a smaller loan is all that we should enter into under the new circumstances".
From what the minister says, I gather that the government does not now know what its own attitude would be in that event?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. Something would
depend on the time. There are things one cannot foresee.

I am only trying to
understand what the position is. I am not trying to embarrass the minister. I should like to know what [DOT] powers are given the government and what the government intends to do with those powers when it has them. My understanding is that if the United States loan is made, this loan will be made in full?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
And these other concessions will also be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
If the United States loan fails, then you look at the whole situation again ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And it is just possible that no further advances might be made-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is possible.
-but likely that some adjustment, some loans within the maximum now provided, would be made available?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, with regard to the last few words, we shall have to consider carefully What we should do. Here is this flow of exports going out of the country and the government has to act with great responsibility about shutting that off.
I am trying to learn what you will do; that is all. You are a little hesitant about being definite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So I should be.

Is it not a fact that a major change in the international situation might involve something larger than the refusal of congress to approve the United States loan? If that loan, to the United Kingdom from the United States does not materialize, is it not quite possible that Great Britain might withdraw from the Bretton Woods agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.
In that event a major change occurs in world trade and commercial arrangements, which weuld necessitate a reconsideration of the whole of our business with the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I should think that would be the thing, because that certainly would necessitate a review of everything we are talking about to-day. If the United States congress refuses to approve the loan and the Bretton Woods agreement falls down, as far as Britain is concerned, it puts the whole world into a chaotic situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

That is understandable, and all I want to know is what the government's policy is with respect to the loan to Great Britain in the event of the United States loan failing. I think I understand the situation, although the minister himself is not very specific.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot be.
He will look at the whole picture again and determine what policy is best in the interests of Canada, of trade, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

Why should the failure of Britain to accept the Bretton Woods agreement influence us in the advancing of this loan? Britain will need the loan in case she
12SS
Loan to United Kingdom

withdraws from Bretton Woods just as much as if she does not. Why should her refusal to accept the Bretton Woods agreement, if it is contingent upon the United States ratifying their loan, have an influence on us and necessitate our reconsidering this loan? That needs to be cleared up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman puts too much stress upon the withdrawal from the Bretton Woods agreement as a factor in the transaction. There will be more serious consequences than those arising from a withdrawal from the Bretton Woods agreement. The United Kingdom would in all probability not be able to reestablish herself as a multilateral trading nation if the United States loan did not go through. This is not simply a question of lending some money to a customer who will turn round and spend that money on your goods. The United States loan and this loan will make it possible for the United Kingdom to get into the way of trading, and this loan by itself cannot accomplish that end. The United States loan is necessary also.
This loan would help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It cannot do the job; it is inadequate. It will take the two of them; and if the other part, the larger part, falls out, then Canada has to consider just what it is in her interests to do. You have then a nation driven into a corner, so to speak, so that it may have to adopt the most restrictive practices; and whether this country would be justified under those circumstances in continuing to advance money to it, having in mind its obligations to its own people, is a question that will have to be considered very carefully at the time.

Britain would be just as likely to be able to repay us this loan if she did not accept Bretton Woods as if she did, would she not? In other words, Britain is just as likely to be able to produce the goods that Canada needs if Britain does not accept Bretton Woods, or if Britain withdraws from Bretton Woods, as she would be if she continued under Bretton Woods. Canada is looking at the ability of Great Britain to repay the loan and if Canada's willingness to advance the loan is contingent upon Great Britain's ability to repay the loan, then it requires some explanation to make it clear to the people why we should not go on with the loan, whether the United States ratifies its loan or does not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ability to repay is not the only consideration. It is the ability of Great Britain to buy in volume, and steadily, in Canada and pay for what she buys in a cur-

rency that is convertible. That is the important thing, and a course of action wihch will probably lead other nations to follow is something that must be considered. I shall not go over all the arguments here. If Great Britain takes a certain course the probability is that the nations of western Europe will follow Great Britain or do the same as Great Britain, and then you have a very serious situation confronting Canada.

The minister, earlier in the discussion, emphasized that in all probability we would not altogether accept goods from Britain in payment of our credits, that we would exchange some of our credits for United States dollars, owing to the fact that, under Bretton Woods, sterling would be convertible into United States dollars. If Bretton Woods fails, sterling will not be convertible. In that event we would not be able to convert our credits into United States dollars and we would have to be willing to accept payment in British goods, which in my opinion would be a good thing in the long run.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to get into an argument on that, but that would upset your plans with somebody else. If you equalize your imports and exports as between Canada and the United Kingdom, are you going to do the same with the United States?

Why should not the United States be willing to buy a sufficient quantity-of goods from Canada to balance trade? There is no reason why we could not have a tripartite agreement. WTe could point out to the United States that we have a surplus credit in England of so many million dollars and we could trade that with the United States.

A few moments ago the minister made some reference to what would happen if the United States loan were not carried. I gathered from what he said that it would affect our supplying of goods to Great Britain under our loan. I have in mind a group of businessmen who are supplying $50 million worth of goods of one kind or another to Great Britain. They will have to make contracts with a lot of other business men in Canada to supply the various parts of the order. From what the minister said I would gather that if the United States loan were defeated the order might be cancelled and that under this loan we would be responsible for a portion of what had already been contracted for in getting the order together for shipment to Great Britain on the understanding that the loan would be ratified. Suppose these business men have spent $10 million on the $50 million order. Am I right

Loan to United Kingdom
in my understanding that if the United States loan is defeated we shall have to cancel the remainder of the order?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is pretty hard to say what would be done in particular situations, or what the effect would be on particular situations. I should not really go farther than reiterate the language which was used in the letter which I wrote to the chancellor of the exchequer, and which he confirmed. I have read it once or twice. I said that this would be a major change; the defeat of the United States loan would be a major change and "it would be necessary forthwith to consider what changes in the provisions of our agreement the two governments should agree to make, subject to such legislative approval as may be necessary". It is difficult to say very much more than that.

I am strongly of opinion that any word which might emanate from anyone whomsoever in Canada who has any responsibility behind him that would in any way interfere with our neighbour's affairs and her relations, with the United Kingdom and give them an excuse to point to any persons in Canada who were doubtful of this particular loan wrould not only have a damaging effect on this very necessary world movement in financial circles but give the isolationists in the United States another opportunity-
It is always the same.

A bird by any other name is just as good-looking-to defeat the purposes of this loan. If such a thing happened we must consider where Canada will end up. At the present time we are all right, but this is of such serious moment to us and to the present financial structure that we should do nothing to jeopardize it. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation said that it is of importance to the world trade position that w-e occupy, and that is right. "VVe should not pry into our neighbour's affairs at -this critical time, because, while we are doing so, our own will be sadly neglected. Why? The minister knows, as do all other hon. members, that if anything happens to the present financial arrangements, within half a decade we shall see a split between the two blocs of currency, namely, the dollar bloc and the sterling bloc. I say to my fellow Canadians that if that happens and any stumbling block is put in the way of multilateral trade that will emanate from this financial arrangement which is attracting the attention of the whole commercial world, Canada, in spite of her wealth of natural resources, will find herself in the
last position so far as her economy is concerned. Why is that so? It is very simple. We all know the spirit of the British people. They will go hungry, and more hungry; they will tighten their belts and get along within the confines of their own financial orbit. They will suffer and suffer more but they will not quit producing. There is more production in Britain per man to-day than in Canada or the United States. As they gradually fill their own shelves which are bereft of most things now and tighten their belts, what will they get? They have 400 million people in Europe waiting for them to increase production. What else have they in the sterling bloc? They have South Africa, New Zealand, Australia and British India. Every time a British pound sterling goes into those areas it buys a pound and quarter's worth of effort in Australia, New Zealand and in the other depreciated currency countries. Where will our trade be while that trade is going on? Britain is recovering. Millions of pounds sterling are lying idle in London and we cannot use them in this country because they are not exchangeable.
Therefore, in the final analyses, if we tamper with this loan, or if anyone helps to defeat this big loan that is now before the congress of the United States we are going to split the world's two currencies; and when we get through spending the extra money which we have in our pockets now, and when the shelves of our country are filled we shall find ourselves, in spite of our God-given resources, the last on the trading list.
I hesitate to take up much of the time of the committee on this subject, and I hesitated to the last minute for fear that any of my words might be used by any of our neighbours to defeat the purpose of the United States loan. May I close with these words:. Let nothing emanate from any Canadian of responsibility which will in any way make our fellow Britons go more hungry, or which will in any way destroy what good might come from this financial arrangement which the nations that think as we do feel is necessary at this time.

I have no desire to delay proceedings, but I think perhaps a word or two more might be said by way of encouragement. From things I have heard and read I have gathered the impression that a good number of people are quite pessimistic with respect to this loan in case the United States should fail to ratify the loan it is proposing to make. In addition to what was said by the minister a moment ago, I think it must be said
Loan to United Kingdom

that if we advance this loan to Great Britain the pounds which we receive from Britain can be converted into the monetary unit of any one of the nations belonging to the sterling bloc. Therefore it seems to me that our chances of receiving repayment for this loan do not depend entirely upon the productive capacity of Great Britain but rather upon the wide and varied productive capacity of all the members of the sterling bloc. Consequently I believe we can afford to go forward pretty confidently, without worrying too greatly whether or not the United States loan is ratified. I do not mean that we do not want the United States to ratify that loan, but I believe there is in this country and in many other members of the British commonwealth too much of a tendency to worry unduly about what the United States does or does not do. The sooner we begin to appreciate that Providence has placed the peoples of the British commonwealth in a preferred position from Ihe point of view of production and trade, the sooner we shall go forward with much greater confidence than we have had manifest for a - long time. So that from what has been said up to the present time I see no reason why Canada should not proceed with her loan, whether or not the United States loan is ratified.

Mr. ILSLEY moved the third reading of the bill.
(Translation) :

Mr. Speaker, I have listened for days to speeches made in this house on the bill under consideration. In spite of the haste with which some of my colleagues would like to see it adopted, it is to my way of thinking, the most important legislation submitted to us since the close of the war.
There is no reason for doubting that the present bill contemplates a gift of nearly half a billion dollars, and, moreover, in spite of all claims to the contrary, this measure will cost the Canadian taxpayer around 66 million dollars annually for the next five years. This matter deserves our close consideration and there is no need to hurry it through. In this connection, I congratulate the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) for his splendid work, for the information he has either given us or obtained for us from the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley).
When I say that we should not hurry this bill through, I have excellent support, for the newspaper Le Droit of April 2, 1946, reports

as follows an interview granted by the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), to a labour organization, the CTCC:
Mr. St. Laurent regrets that the CTCC is so definitely opposed to the loan to Great Britain, but he adds that, to a certain extent, he understands the position they are taking on the matter, because he himself was convinced, only after having spent three or four weeks in discussing the subject with the British delegation and the North American experts, that this loan was the best policy to insure us against unemployment, trade stagnation and a recurrence of depression in Canada.
It is therefore understandable, Mr. Speaker, when the right hon. Minister of Justice had to spend three or four weeks in consultation with experts to grasp the full scope of this financial agreement, that the house should consider it carefully and take all the time it needs for doing so, in order to be in a position to adopt or reject it, as the case may be.
Mr. Speaker, the most often repeated argument, in the course of this debate, has been that the present agreement is bound to be helpful to both our tra.de and our industries. It cannot be denied that if we open credits to foreign countries we shall have no trouble in selling the goods we produce. That brings up , the picture of a merchant who, to boost his trade, after having stored a large stock, would one day, tell his customers: "I am opening, for each of you, a credit account of S10,000; all I ask you is to make your purchases at my store." In the few days or w'eeks following that offer, the business of that merchant would be very brisk; you may be sure of that; however, the state of his business would be pitiable at the end of three or four weeks: he would inevitably be faced with bankruptcy. Who, I ask you, would have benefited from the action of that merchant? The go-betweens, the distributors of the goods, those who, in the case now under consideration, we call the financial organization of the country.
There is no doubt that, having accumulated, as the Minister of Finance pointed out the other day, wealth to the amount of ten billion dollars during the war, the high financiers and trusts wish to keep on doing so; that is the reason why they are unanimous in their support of the loan to England. However, when the interest become due, the annual amount of 66 million dollars will have to be paid out of the public funds, that is to say, the taxpayer will have to pay for the gift we propose to make now.
In the opinion of some-it is right here in the statement made by the right hon. the Minister of Justice which I have just read- this loan is an insurance policy. Considering the premium, the cost of such an insurance

Loan to United Kingdom
policy is prohibitive. Some newspapers and certain hon. members here in the house have used other arguments; those who object to the loan, for instance,-it is the same old story which we have heard so often-are considered as isolationists. Mr. Speaker, the strongest argument in favour of the loan has been put forward by a Quebec newspaperman who reports daily in certain Quebec newspapers; he used two columns of a newspaper to ax-plain an argument based on the following statement: Those who object to the loan are all demagogues. When one can think of no better argument to defend such a measure, it is high time that it be carefully studied, because it cannot be very sound.
This is claimed to be a loan and it is always referred to as such. But the Minister of Finance himself said a moment ago that the bill now before the house calls for a gift to England of half a billion dollars, through cancellation of a debt owed us by that country. When the lender in search of a borrower cannot force his loans on anyone without paying the interest himself, without disbursing his own money, his actions are contrary to all sound economical and financial principles, although I am not very conversant with such matters. I always thought, Mr. Speaker, that lending was supposed to be a profitable business; however, if we have to pay interest ourselves, it cannot be advantageous to us.
It is evident-this has often been stated both in the house and outside-that this agreement is a consequence of the war and of the policies pursued during the last few years. So that if we must as an aftermath of the war, grant a loan which, as I have already said, will cost a lot of the taxpayers' money, whilst during the war some people were allowed to accumulate iff excess of ten billion dollars-the Minister of Finance has admitted so himself-would it not be simpler to levy this money from those who have profited from the war? Were this to be the government's policy, I know not a single Canadian who would object to such a course of action in order to help Great Britain. Let the government take the money where it lies, without compelling the soldiers who were overseas for four or five years to pay interest on the capital they fought to preserve. We really took part in that war to safeguard our economic and democratic system, and those who fought the war and are now coming back to Canada will have to contribute their share of interest on those billions. This bill is unfair to them, as well as to all taxpayers. For those reasons, I shall fight it to the last.

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fair for the second reading of bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

subtopic: COMMISSIONS TO AGENTS IN CONNECTION WITH SALE OP WHEAT
speechtext:
I shall sum up in five minutes my main contentions of last Tuesday. First of all, I pointed out that my chief concern with regard to the amendment was with reference to the wheat board and not the grain exchange. As I pointed out before, the grain exchange is not mentioned in the bill. This is simply a bill to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and I was sincerely of the opinion that this amendment would weaken the position of the Canadian wheat board to such an extent that it was my duty to oppose it. I said also that according to my reading of this amendment the effect would be to expropriate most if not all of the country elevators throughout western Canada, because, as I interpret the amendment, the Canadian wheat board, which is the instrument of the government and as such should be considered as the government, has to take over all marketing facilities.
In my home town there is an elevator owned and operated by the farmers, and if a wheat transaction were to take place in that town the Canadian wheat board in Winnipeg would have to send a civil servant, an employee, pay him his salary and expenses and provide him with a car to come to that town for the sole purpose of transacting a wheat sale ranging anywhere from, I can imagine, five or six up to a thousand bushels of wheat, whereas at the present time the Canadian wheat board can simply call the elevator man on the telephone and ask him to carry out the transaction for the wheat board, and the whole thing can be done at the cost of a few cents.
I contend that this amendment is too loose to serve the purpose the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has in mind and it would be unwise to proceed with it. I pointed out the other day that, as regards the contention of the sponsor of the bill that the board was paying for unnecessary services,
I was unable to discover from any reports of the wheat board that they were doing so. However, if that is the case-I do not know and I have not been able to find out-the best way in which to vindicate the charge

Canadian Wheat Board
is to bring the whole matter before the committee on agriculture, have the officials come here, question them, and get the neces-. sary information from them. I respectfully suggested on Tuesday last that we submit the whole matter to the committee on agriculture. This amendment, to put it in a nutshell, is purely and simply a form of socialism of a most expensive kind, and I strongly oppose it.
As far as the grain exchange is concerned, and it is extremely incidental in this bill, I for one do not believe that we should to-day return to the old system of marketing as we knew it in the past. I have here a humorous clipping which I shall read to the house, not because it is authentic but because it reflects to some extent the attitude of the farmer and the attitude he had at that time. It gives a definition of wheat.
Wheat, it appears, is a seed that is planted and grown to keep the producer broke and the buyer crazy. It is planted in the spring, mortgaged in the summer, and lost in the fall. Its quality varies according to the amount of rain or frost experienced during the growing season. A man who can guess nearest to this quality is called a wheat grader by the public and a fool by the farmer.
The price of -wheat is determined at primary market. It goes down when one has bought, and up when one has sold. All of which reminds us of the story of the buyer working for a group of millers who came west to watch the wheat markets. After a few days he wired his principals to this effect:
"Some think wheat will go down and some think it will go up. I think so, too. Whatever you will do will be wrong. Act at once.
This is not accurate, but those who have known conditions in western Canada during the thirties, and when they had to depend entirely on the supply and demand for the price of wheat, will realize that it reflects to a certain extent the predicament of the farmers at the time.. That situation has been relieved by the establishment of the wheat board. I repeat that I feel strongly in regard to the Canadian wheat board, and any amendment that would tend to weaken its position or worsen the situation I feel it my duty to oppose.

tied because he was working under arrangements which were made in 1903. If farmers carried on their business like that I do not know where they would be to-day. To be progressive, business must keep up with the times. One could compare the system which has been laid down for the wheat board to follow with a farmer driving twenty-five miles into town with a horse and buggy or ploughing with oxen. They ploughed with oxen in the west in 1903. The wheat board of to-day operates under arrangements which were followed in 1803.
If this bill were passed it would give the wheat board power to do business the way in which they should do it in a modern world. It would streamline the board instead of tying, its hands. To-day the wheat board is following the custom that was in vogue thirty-five or forty years ago. It should be changed. I have great respect for the wheat board. I have told the minister that before and I know he believes me when I say it. They have done a good job. It is unfortunate that they were not given the chance to do with rye what they have done with wheat, namely, stabilize the price. The man who eats rye bread to-day is paying around $2.90 a bushel for it. That is a deplorable state of affairs. The farmers receives one dollar and some odd cents for it and after the operations that it goes through the poor man has to pay $2.80 or $2.90 for it. That sort of thing should not be permitted in a modern world. But because of the way in which the wheat board's hands are tied they have to follow that system.
I have said that this group is in favour of the wheat board. We hope that it will be continued. I should like to see this bill pass to give the board more power than it has ever had because its hands are tied to the old methods that are employed by organizations which to-day are parasites on the backs of the farmers. Anybody who gets paid for a service that is not necessary is a parasite. We have to-day a lot of parasites in the grain trade. Let us hope that the wheat board will be supported in every corner of the house because it is the right and proper way to market grain. speechtext:
I am going to support this measure but not for the reasons advanced by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras). I do not agree with him that the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has any great claim to the philosophy of socialism. In this respect he is simply following out what for many years has been in the minds of a great many people in western Canada.
Canadian Wheat Board

I wish to point out to the house that there is a considered reason why we support this method of selling wheat. I have no hesitation in saying that whether it is in the mind of the mover of the bill or not, it is certainly in my mind, that this will help to do the very thing which the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) mentioned, namely, eliminate completely from the scene of grain marketing in Canada the Winnipeg grain exchange.
The considered opinions of the people who have supported this measure in the west dates back to the years of the first world war when they had their first experience with it. In 1917-18 the government of the day in its wisdom decided to stop the marketing of grain through the futures or speculative system. They set up a commission to handle the buying and they fixed a price at that time. The following year they felt that they could improve on that particular method and they set up the Canada wheat board which operated until August, 1919. They established a new system of marketing grain in this country, one which had not been tried out before, and which few people would have had the temerity to recommend to the people at that time. Although few people might have had it in mind, the government of the day set up the wheat board to operate in such a way that it made an initial payment at the time of delivery by the wheat producer. The board then gave him a participation certificate, and when the grain was sold through the various buying agencies to the buying or importing countries across the sea and the returns were made and the cost of operating the board was deducted the balance was payable at so much a bushel on each grade of grain when the books were closed.
That was something which pleased a great many farmers. I am not going to try to mislead the house or the people from eastern or other parts of Canada by saying that it pleased every farmer. Farmers are much like anybody else; they differ in their opinions on how to do things. Some of them like the idea of speculation; some of them like to be completely separate and alone or away from any particularly close association in the doing of their business with other people.
When I speak at this time I am speaking from an intimate knowledge of the workings of the minds and the thoughts of those farmers who believe in organization for their own protection. No doubt the others I have mentioned will have numerous champions in this house. Of course they have a perfect right to their own point of view.

When the wheat board of the first world war ceased to operate and the speculative market reopened, the price quoted was about $2.78 a bushel. I do not have that old history with me at the moment; if anyone looks it up he may find I am out a fraction of a cent or a cent, but I think that was the figure. I know that within one year after the Winnipeg grain exchange was opened and speculation was in full force again the price of wheat dropped by $1.60. If you can do quick mental arithmetic you can subtract $1.60 from $2.78 and you will have the figure. Furthermore, by the fall of 1923 when the crop came on the market, wheat was selling at just a little over $1 a bushel, while some grades were considerably below that figure.
I am giving the house this history, because it is important to know the background of the demand which as best I can I am helping to urge in this house, as expressed in this bill. This is a bill, not a resolution; sometimes I become confused, because I am new to this sort of procedure. When we in the west found this condition obtaining on the open, speculative market, represented by the grain exchange, we commenced to organize ourselves, after first having asked the government here in Ottawa to reinstitute the wheat board. For its own reasons the government was unable or unwilling to do so. We need not go into that matter. Governments change; minds change. At that time no doubt they felt they were right, but in any event they did not set up the wheat board again, and as a result we had to organize ourselves. In that organization I must admit that we had a great deal to learn. Like this House of Commons here, we did not know everything back in 1923. Neither we nor they know everything yet, but we have all had twenty-three years of experience since that time.
We went on to organize the great farm marketing institutions, the wheat pools, operating on a voluntary basis somewhat along the lines of the wheat board. In the years 1923 to 1929, when Europe was being rebuilt and rehabilitated after the war, the thing worked fairly well; but when the world collapse came in 1929 and 1930 we found that we were not strong enough, organized in one country alone, even though we were well organized, to withstand the impact of world conditions. At the same time we found that the speculative market was much more ineffective than the wheat pools in maintaining and stabilizing prices for the farmers. We all know the history of what was done by the government of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett at

Canadian Wheat Board
that time. In their own way they tried to maintain what they believed was a free enterprise system in the marketing of grain. They would not interfere with the speculative channels, but they had to do something, and they did perform what were called stabilization operations, which were not very successful but which did help to a certain extent. That gave an indication that these things could be controlled. The farm organizations were continuously pressing for the establishment of a wheat board, with the sole idea of eliminating the grain exchange.
Before getting this far I should have mentioned that there was a certain definite philosophy behind the cooperative grain marketing organizations formed in 1923. On the fly leaf of their handbook you will find, among others, these words:
... to eliminate manipulation, speculation and waste and all unnecessary transactions in the marketing of grain, and to preserve for the producer and consumer their proper profits and economies . . .
That word "profits" will indicate that we were not socialists then, and not all of those in the movement are socialists even yet. They were trying to maintain their proper profits and economies. That was the slogan then, and those words are still on the fly-leaf of the handbook of Canadian cooperative wheat producers. After that we got the wheat board. I do not want to recite a whole lot of history, but in getting that wheat board in 1935 one of the things the farm organizations particularly wanted was a committee to assist and advise the wheat board in the marketing of wheat and the fixing of a price for it There was a great deal of controversy and a great deal of opposition from the operators on the Winnipeg grain exchange to the fixing of that price. Again I do not wish to criticize any individuals here. People did and supported what they thought was proper at that time, but again I am speaking from the point of view of the organized farmers, who wanted the price fixed somewhere near the cost of production. At that time the people who sat in this House of Commons were not convinced that this was a very good idea, but if I gauge the temper of this house to-night, a great many hon. members would violently oppose the removal of controls at the present time so that prices would move either upward or downward at the will of speculators. In any event, at that time they wanted stabilization in the matter of farm products, based on something like the actual cost of production to the farm operator.
So we got the wheat board, and ever since that time we have been attempting to have the board cease using any of those agencies whose 63260-821
operations might be included in the "un-~ necessary transactions" mentioned in the' quotation I gave from the fly-leaf of hand-~ book No. 1 of the Canadian cooperative wheat producers. We were not successful; the" organizations are still carrying on. But other-organizations which at that time had not seen

the picture have now learned that this is' important. For instance, since that time we have seen the organization of the Canadian federation of agriculture. That federation has a twelve-point programme, and point No. 6 is this:
The establishment of a permanent national wheat marketing policy to give encouragement and leadership to development of an international wheat agreement and work out price arrangements which would prevent wide fluctuations.
That means negotiated prices. It does not mean prices arrived at by speculation on the part of some persons who desire to buy or sell options and put up a margin. Point No. 7 states:
Establishment of the Canadian wheat board as the "sole institution" for the marketing of Canadian cereal crops.
In the early days of this organization many people even in the west did not see this picture clearly. Now it is seen and understood by people all over Canada, because the Canadian federation of agriculture represents farm organizations of all kinds, and they are not all cooperatives. There are some organizations which do not claim to be cooperatives but simply to represent the interests of some particular type of farm industry across this dominion. These people belonging to this organization have joined the wheat pools and the organized farmers of the west in endorsing this policy. Some hon. members were-here in the early days of 1942, when a delegation came to Ottawa. They will remember the representations along those lines which, were made at that time. Now we have another world-wide organization in connection-with which I want to remind hon. members of point No. 6 in the recommendations of the federation of agriculture, having to do-with the development of an international world wheat agreement to work out prices. Three years ago we had the Hot Springs food conference, which last fall was crystallized in the united nations food and agriculture organization. One of their plans, as set out in article I of the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations Act,, said:
The organization shall promote and, where-appropriate, shall recommend national and international action with respect to (d) the improvement of the processing, marketing and. distribution of food and agricultural products..
Canadian Wheat Board

There is no question that all are agreed that the organized methods of marketing cereal products or wheat itself, and including oats and barley to the extent to which they are handled, through the wheat board, has been an improvement. Even the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) agreed to-night that the wheat board has done a magnificent job, and we are very proud of our part in the west in helping to promote the work of that board. I agree with the hon. member that it has brought about a vast improvement in the marketing of cereal products. It has brought advantage to the farmer who has produced those cereals, to the nation of which the farmer is a citizen, and to the purchasers of those products.
When we have something working well, why is it not a good thing to improve it as much as possible? We believe that if the wheat board is given authority to set up its own organization, and if it has not to use unnecessary institutions, there will be an improvement in the situation which will be of value to all concerned.
In the early days many organizations had not agreed that this was a good thing. We had our rural municipal associations which were not yet convinced. Now the rural municipal association, in Saskatchewan at least, *would endorse this policy. We have another "big agricultural association in Saskatchewan, and I should like to emphasize to any who may be listening that the organized agricultural societies of Saskatchewan are not cooperative institutions. They do not bear the name "cooperative"; their philosophy is not based upon the cooperative philosophy in trading. Many of their members believe in it, but the organizations themselves are just as they were when they were created many years ago, namely distinctly local agricultural societies organized and joined together for the purpose of improving production of agricultural products.
They, too, have advanced and learned. They, too, in the past have been the victims of unfortunate circumstances. They, too, are comprised of intelligent me'n. Indeed, right in this corner of the chamber sits an hon. member, namely the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. Townley-Smith) who is a high official in that organization. He can vouch for what I am going to say about them. Some of them may believe in speculation, while others believe in cooperative marketing; but all believe in the improvement of production methods. Last January they held a meeting of the Saskatchewan agricultural association in Saskatoon, and at that meeting passed

a resolution containing six points. The first point, considered by them the most important -there are others, but I shall mention only the one because it has reference of the matter before the house to-night-states;
The Canadian wheat board should be the sole marketing agency for coarse grains as well as wheat.
If they passed a resolution like that it is obvious they are not asking to have the wheat board the sole marketing agency, and then expecting that wheat board to diffuse its responsibility and use unnecessary marketing agencies which would eliminate or to a large extent nullify the meaning of the word ''sole" in the resolution.
I make these observations this evening, through you, Mr. Speaker, in order to try to convince the house that the bill before it is an important one and one which has received the support of organized farmers from western Canada, because the experience in past years has convinced them that such action is necessary.
Someone will say, "All these farm organizations do not believe in it." I say that all the big ones do, and that many of the smaller ones do. I cannot vouch for all the smaller ones. However, the ones I have mentioned here this evening have stated their official ideas in the matter, and because of that I do not think there should be any hesitation whatsoever in allowing this bill to come to a vote.
I could give a number of quotations, but if I do not conclude soon I may be accused of having talked out the very thing I wish to support. I hope the house will vote on the 'bill to-night, and thus give the necessary impetus and encouragement to the producers of western Canada, thereby showing them that the rest of Canada is behind their efforts to improve their own conditions.

Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the terms of the bill I should like to make it clear that so far as I am concerned I am now, and have been ever since I have been in public life, favourable to the policy of the wheat board handling wheat and coarse grains, and doing so exclusively. There can be no doubt as to my stand on the part of anyone who has followed my speeches in the matter.
In regard to this particular bill, however, there seems to be some confusion as to what it attempts to do. For example, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) said that the hands of the wheat board were tied, and that it was the purpose of the bill to untie them. Then the hon. member for Svift Current (Mr. MAY 7, 1940
Canadian W.heat Board
Bentley) said that the purpose of the bill was to give the wheat board the right to set up its own agency, so that it would not have to employ private grain agencies to handle wheat, and this would mean that it would not have to employ cooperative agencies for that purpose.
I believe the wise procedure is to look at the terms of the bill. Section 8 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act states the following in paragraph (i):
In selling and disposing of wheat as by this act provided, to utilize and employ without discrimination such marketing agencies, including commission merchants, brokers, elevator men, exporters and other persons engaged in or operating facilities for the selling and handling of wheat, as the board in its discretion may determine.
(j) to offer continuously wheat for sale in the markets of the world through the established channels: Provided that the board may, if in its opinion any existing agencies are not operating satisfactorily, take such steps as it deems expedient to establish, utilize and employ its own or other marketing agencies or channels.
The purpose of the bill is to repeal those very sections which give the wheat board power to employ any marketing agencies it sees fit; and if it finds that any of those marketing agencies are not operating satisfactorily, to utilize and employ its own marketing agencies. So that the act as it stands to-day gives the wheat board the full power either to use existing marketing agencies or to set up its own. I cannot see the cogency of any argument which says, "We want to give the wheat board power to set up its own agencies", and then bring in a bill, and support it, which repeals the section which gives that very power.
Among the great marketing agencies operating in western Canada are the great grain marketing pools, the cooperative grain marketing organizations. They are the ones which are handling to a great extent the grain of western Canada. I take it from the bill presented by the hon. member that he would deprive these great cooperative marketing agencies of the right to handle the grain of the farmers for the wheat board.
As far as I am concerned, and as I said at the beginning, while I am in favour of the wheat board having the exclusive right to handle the grain of the western farmer-and in that I include rye; I have made representations to the Minister of Trade and Commerce accordingly-I would much rather see this grain handled by it through the cooperative organizations which have been set up to take it from the farmer, to ship it to the east, to handle it in the terminal elevators and to Ethip it abroad than by any agency of government, no matter how well it is handled. I have
no hesitation in saying that, whenever it is a choice between cooperation and state socialism,
I will take cooperation every time.

by what the law says, not by what is said by the person who introduced it. That is very funny indeed. That is just about as foolish as introducing a bill which does exactly the opposite to what the hon. member says he intended to do. The watchword of every man representing a grain farming constituency in this house should be, in the light of the grand record of the wheat board, "Hands off the wheat board; do not interfere with them; give them a chance to carry out the work they have been doing so well in the past and, if they require it, give them even more power to deal with grain that they have no right to deal with exclusively to-day." In other words, add to their rights; do not interfere with them.
In regard to the policy which is being enforced under the present wheat board act, I would say at this particular stage when there seems to be some doubt as to what the proper policy should be in regard to farm products:

I think the farmer is just as much entitled to a reasonable minimum price for his product as the working man is entitled to a fixed minimum wage. The farmer is just as much entitled to a fair share of the national income consistent with the amount of work he does and the amount he has invested and so on as any other particular group in the community. This government in introducing and having passed by this house the Agricultural Prices Support Act has given its approval to such a policy. I should like to put on the record section 9, subsection 2, of that act which was passed in 1944 and which, I take it, is still the policy of the government as enacted by this parliament. This subsection reads:
(2) In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection one of this section, the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
There is a definite pronouncement of a fair deal for the farmers of this country. As far as I am concerned I hope and believe the government will never waiver from its policy of a fair and just deal for the farmer.

It has been proclaimed in part already and the chairman of the board is already functioning.
With regard to wheat, I take it that the policy, of a minimum price must be carried out by the wheat board. For that reason I should like to see the wheat board continue with full power, or with added powers if those are needed to discharge fully the obligation which this parliament has assumed toward the great agricultural industry of this country.
Some people may ask why the farmer should have fixed prices for his products. One of the first reasons I would suggest-and I can speak with a great deal of feeling because all my life I have been either a farmer or closely in touch with farmers-is that the hazards of farming are enough for a farmer to contend with without having to be faced with a fall in the prices which will wipe out, even though he has a good crop, what he has the right to expect from his months of hard work. In that connection I wish to quote from a speech of the president of the Canadian federation of agriculture to that organization in January, 1945, which I commend to the consideration of the house:

Canadian Wheat Board
To the people of Canada not engaged in agriculture we say, in all seriousness: If costs of distribution are to be continued at approximately present margins; if capital employed in agriculture is to continue to receive rewards on the same basis as in recent years; and more particularly if the greater part of industry in Canada is to hang on to the protection it has enjoyed, then equality of exchange for agriculture definitely means relatively high prices for agricultural products and correspondingly high retail food prices.
If most other industries and groups persist in clinging to practices and privileges designed to hold their prices or rewards for services on a high level, then in all justice agricultural prices must be placed on the same level.
Please note, agriculture is not choosing that level, nor do we recommend it. But if Canada decides to maintain the greater part of her economy on that higher level, and to pay the farmer on the basis of a cheap food policy, the result will be to exploit the purchasing power and living standards of people living on the land, bring tragedy to agriculture, and eventually the tragedy of unemployment and depression to the nation as a whole. A cheap food policy at the expense of agriculture will be bad business for everybody and a costly blunder for Canada in the end.
What is the policy in regard to wheat? I have heard it said on the floor of this house that a very high price was obtained for wheat following the last war, but in case I have not time to read the quotation I wished to read in regard to this, let me preface what I am going to say by this. The farm leaders of western Canada have upheld the policy of price stabilization and loyally supported it.

That is in accordance with the policy of the government and laid down in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. In this regard, however, I would say this. One of the things that the farmers of western Canada feel most strongly about is that while they are not asking for the last cent they can get for their wheat in the day of need of the consumer of bread, they do say this, that so far as the internal price of wheat is concerned, when you take wheat from the farmer at SI .25 a bushel to make it into bread in Canada and when you are selling the wheat abroad at $1.55 a bushel, you are asking wheat farmers to subsidize the consumer of bread in this country to the extent of thirty cents a bushel on between forty and fifty million bushels of
wheat. That' amounts to a subsidy by the farmers of this country to the bread-eaters of this country of from $12,000,000 to $15,000,000.
The farmer says this, that if the price of his fuel oil and gasoline is to rise two cents a gallon and the price of his farm implements by 12Vo per cent, that policy of the farmer subsidizing the bread-eater of this country is one which should be reconsidered. If we are to have cheap bread, to which the farmer has no objection, the nation as a whole should pay that subsidy to provide it and not the farmer.
In order to bear out my statement that the farmers of this country have loyally supported the policy of price stabilization and do not seek to exact the last cent out of the present difficult food situation, I should like to read to the house from a recent broadcast by Mr. Wesson, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) to-day make some reference to the amount which the farmer got for his wheat following the last war. Let me first give the figures on that.
The Winnipeg market, in September, 1920, showed an average cash price for that month for wheat of S2.73j, cents a bushel. That is very fine. But by next fall, in November, 1921, the average price had dropped to S1.10J a bushel, and the farmers of western Canada, having been once bitten under that sort of system, are not going, if they can avoid it, to permit themselves to be bitten again. Let me now read what Mr. Wesson said on that point in a broadcast on April 2 of this year:
There is quite an agitation in some quarters to-day that wheat prices ought to be much higher than they are at the present time because of the acute wheat shortage. No one will disagree that higher prices could be secured under present conditions, but don't be fooled by this dangling bait that is being placed before you, because the advocates who are using so much lip-service to-day have a very different motive. They want to get back to the old order of things. The free and open market system of trading, with high sounding phrases like the inexorable law of supply and demand.
But, while the exponents of higher prices today are very eager in the interests of the farmer that he should get higher prices, you will notice that they go no further than the present time, and you know, and I know, that based on past experience, if we had no protection but the much vaunted open market system, when the supply position changed on the swing of the pendulum to the opposite extreme, we could quite easily get back to the same position as in the black years of the 1930's. when wheat on this same open market went down to less than 40 cents a bushel.

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 3, consideration in committee of bill No. 7, respecting citizenship, nationality, and naturalization and status of aliens-Mr. Martin- Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
When the committee rose the other night the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) had moved an amendment which I think I should now read to the committee. The hon. member moved that section 10 be amended as follows:
That the following words be added to the section as subsection 6:	"Such certificate of
citizenship shall be deemed to include a Bill of Eights as follows:
1.	Freedom of religion, freedom of speech, and the right to peaceable assembly are assured.
2.	Habeas corpus shall not be suspended except by parliament.
3.	No one shall be required to give evidence before any tribunal or commission at any time if denied counsel or other constitutional safeguards."

subtopic: NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND STATUS OF ALIENS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend this evening to make a formal speech in support of the amendment that you have just read. This amendment is not meant to be all-exclusive, nor is it meant to

be all-inclusive. My first suggestion is that if the Secretary of State accepts the principle of the need in this country of a bill of rights signifying what citizenship stands for, then possibly the best means whereby that result could be effected would be to set up a committee of the house. It would not take very long for that committee to meet and it would afford an opportunity to exchange ideas among the various groups in the house and thereby evolve a bill of rights which would be acceptable to all, and one which would carry into effect the highest principles of citizenship.
I realize that there are many who say that all the rights referred to in the amendment are now in effect and that there is no necessity to have a bill of rights in Canada, that the great principles of Magna Charta, the Petition of Right, Habeas Corpus and the Bill of Rights are part and parcel of the law of this land and that, except in war time, they have not been interfered with and therefore it is not necessary to have a bill of rights.
But may I point out that during recent years, and particularly since 1914 when the War Measures Act was passed, there has been a trend and tendency in this country to diminish and attenuate rights ordinarily comprised in citizenship, and I proposed the amendment for the purpose of having parliament determine once and for all that a stop be put to the continuance of any such tendency or trend in this land.
The citizenship bill as a whole has received support from all sides of the house, and with the exception of one provision in the bill, there has been almost unanimous support of the need for it and of its terms. I am not going to make this evening anything in the nature of a partisan speech, for I believe that this is a matter which deserves the serious consideration of all members in all parts of the house.
My appeal at the very outset is that the minister, in order to round out the work already begun by him under this citizenship bill, should complete that work now by having parliament declare once and for all the rights that are incident to citizenship in this country. Only recently, all too recently, the people of Canada have become liberty-conscious by reason of what has taken place in connection with the espionage investigation.
While at the beginning of that investigation there were those in Canada who said, "After all, what is being done can do no harm because those against whom the proceedings are being taken belong to a philosophy alien to ours", in recent days Canadians on every hand are saying. "Well, if they can do it in the case of those whose philosophy is antagonistic to

Canadian Citizenship
ours, is there any reason why the government could not do the same thing under order in council against other minorities?"
It is for that reason that the problem has become of great significance. I believe that a matter of primary importance in parliament is to assure the maximum preservation of civil liberties. We became accustomed to the diminution of those liberties during the war when rights were abridged and terminated in many cases because the survival of the nation was more important than the preservation or survival of democratic symbolism.
This citizenship bill, in order to carry out the hopes of those who have given it their support, must assure that in this country there shall be no superior class of citizenship and that citizenship shall not be based on race, creed or colour, nor shall there be any first or second-class citizenship. Let there be no mistake about this. I am unalterably opposed to any alteration or diminution of the rights of Canadian citizens by order in council independently of parliament; for history shows that if you permit the rights of a citizen to be impinged upon, regardless of who that citizen may be, every other person is a step nearer to the loss of his rights, since infringements upon democratic rights have no limits except in the limitations imposed by the vigilance of the people. History proves, too, that when minority rights are interfered with, or when the prerogative rights of individuals are invaded, it is not long before few dare to conform but to the desires of the majority, and often those who exact oppression on minorities are themselves the first victims. Liberty is not something that can be purchased for all time. There are not several kinds of liberty; there is only one liberty, namely, the liberty based on law and under law.
I have said that lately there has been a definite trend away from the principles of liberty. The War Measures Act remains on the statute books of this country. So long as it is on the statute books there is no reason why governments, if they so choose, might not create emergencies real or apprehended, thereby permitting them to commit arbitrary acts under its powers.
This parliament should endeavour to assure that never again, excepting by parliament, shall the rights of individuals be reduced or entirely done away with. In connection with the order in council which dealt with the espionage problem, the right of habeas corpus was done away with as directly as though the order in council so provided, because that order in council stated that every person held, regardless of the circumstances under which he was held, was deemed to be under lawful 63260-83
arrest. I am going to refer to one or two sections of these great bulwarks of liberty of Magna Charta, the Petition of Right, the Habeas Corpus Act and the Bill of Rights, and leave it to the committee to appreciate the extent to which these rights have been interfered with in the recent order in council.
So far as Magna Charta is concerned article 40 states:
To no one will we sell, to no one will we deny, or delay right or justice.
One has only to recall what took place a few short weeks ago when men were denied the right to present their cases, were held without charge against them and were denied the opportunity of having counsel during the proceedings of the investigation to realize that these rights have been denied.
Then there is the Petition of Right. That petition of 1628 provided one thing more importantly than anything else, namely, that no one should be held unless there was against him a charge known to law. The Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 was entirely removed by the order in council passed in October last, and that removal became part of the law of this land under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act, although in passing that act parliament thought it was passing an act in regard to economic matters instead of matters respecting the liberty of the subject.
Finally there is the Bill of Rights of 1689. It contains certain principles there that are applicable to this discussion. They were condemned at that time, and yet they were adopted in 1945 and 1946. One of them reads as follows:
That the pretended power of suspending of laws or the execution of laws by regal authority without consent of parliament is illegal.
I have already pointed out what was done in reference to habeas corpus by the executive. The Bill of Rights states in part:
That the pretended power of dispensing with laws or the execution of law's by regal authority as it hath been assumed and exercised of late is illegal.
That the commission for erecting the lay court of commissioners for ecclesiastical causes and all other commissions and courts of like nature are illegal and pernicious.
Furthermore, it sets out that every man shall receive his right to his day in court and without unnecessary delay.
As I said a moment ago, I did not state that the Bill of Rights as set forth in the amendment is all-exclusive or all-inclusive. In paragraph 7 it asks for a declaration that:
Freedom of religion, freedom of speech and the right to peaceable assembly are assured.

Canadian Citizenship
